analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 3, 2019 and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes on very large transfers of wealth between generations. These taxes apply only to estates above roughly $11 million per person, so repeal would cut taxes exclusively for the heirs of the wealthiest few thousand families each year, while removing billions of dollars in annual federal revenue that everyone else would have to make up through deficits or other taxes. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates in the country. Under 2019 rules the estate tax only applied to estates worth more than about $11.4 million per person, and only a few thousand estates a year actually paid it. Repealing it, along with the gift and generation-skipping taxes, means those families could pass on unlimited wealth tax-free.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
The repeal takes effect for deaths and gifts after the date of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and by extension all other taxpayers, who would either absorb tens of billions of dollars in lost annual revenue as higher deficits or pay for the repeal through other taxes or spending cuts.
analysis.who_pays_short: All other taxpayers through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The repeal applies to the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes together, so the largest fortunes could be transferred across generations without any transfer tax at all.
Because these taxes are paid only on very large estates, the direct benefit of repeal goes to a small share of very wealthy households, while the lost revenue is spread across everyone else.

Even supporters of reform acknowledge the current tax already exempts very large estates; under 2019 rules a couple could pass on over $22 million before any tax was owed, which is why only a few thousand estates paid it each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed for a narrow group: the families who actually owe estate tax are a few thousand of the country's largest estates each year, and they would save millions each, while the general public would bear the cost through lost revenue. The good-faith case for repeal is that some family farms and small businesses can face real paperwork or liquidity pressure at death, but the bill takes the bluntest possible approach — full repeal for the largest fortunes — rather than addressing that narrower problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 3, 2019, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2019 by Rep. Mac Thornberry, with Rep. Dan Newhouse listed as the original cosponsor, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

The complete action history shows only two steps: introduction and the committee referral. No hearing, markup, floor vote, or any further action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The Ways and Means Committee was the only committee of referral, so the bill's fate rested entirely with that committee, which never acted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax stays in place, so the Treasury keeps collecting revenue from the largest estates, and ordinary taxpayers avoid picking up the lost revenue. The wealthiest households are the losers — they remain no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry

for.name: Rep. Dan Newhouse
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as the original cosponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party signed on.

against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. All sponsorship came from Republicans (Thornberry plus three cosponsors, all R), and the Democratic chair of the sole committee of referral never moved it, but no recorded vote exists to show how the chambers would have split.

industries.note: Repeal would let heirs to estates above roughly $11 million per person — a few thousand families a year — inherit without any federal estate tax, while the lost revenue would fall on everyone else through deficits or other taxes. The industry's gain here is directly the public's cost.
Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would remove most of the compliance work around large wealth transfers; the savings to clients come at the cost of federal revenue.

The standard argument for repeal is relief for heirs facing liquidity pressure at death, but current exemptions already cover most estates, so most of the benefit of this bill would go to the largest fortunes rather than to typical family businesses.
